title: Touch Receptors
intro: Touch starts at the endings of low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR) neurons in the skin, whose cell bodies sit in the dorsal root ganglia. In the hairless (glabrous) skin of the hand, four classes of afferent fibre, each with its own end organ, split touch into pressure, vibration, slip and stretch. Each class differs in how fast it adapts and how large its receptive field is, and together their spike trains carry enough information for fine manipulation within tens of milliseconds.

items: SA1 afferents with Merkel cell complexes: slowly adapting, small receptive fields, high spatial resolution; they encode pressure, edges, curvature and the shape of Braille dots. Merkel cells are themselves mechanosensitive through the Piezo2 channel and help set the sustained response (Woo et al. 2014; Maksimovic et al. 2014).

RA1 (FA1) afferents with Meissner corpuscles: rapidly adapting, small receptive fields; they respond to skin motion and low-frequency vibration (flutter) and are important for detecting slip during grip.
SA2 afferents with Ruffini-like endings: slowly adapting, large receptive fields, sensitive to skin stretch; they signal hand shape and the direction of forces.

RA2 (FA2) afferents with Pacinian corpuscles: very rapidly adapting, very large receptive fields, exquisitely sensitive to high-frequency vibration (best around 200 to 300 Hz, down to nanometre displacements). They carry the vibrations of tools and fine textures.
Numbers: roughly 17,000 mechanoreceptive afferents innervate the glabrous skin of one human hand, densest at the fingertips (Johansson & Vallbo 1979).

Hairy skin adds other classes: hair follicle afferents of several types and slow, unmyelinated C-tactile afferents that respond best to gentle stroking and are thought to carry the pleasant, social side of touch (Abraira & Ginty 2013).

Coding: tactile afferents encode fast. The relative timing of the first spikes across a population signals the direction of fingertip forces and the shape of a contacted surface before rates have had time to build up (Johansson & Birznieks 2004), and the precise timing of Pacinian and RA spikes carries texture information (Weber et al. 2013).

Kim, Sripati and Bensmaia (2010): each afferent as a linear filter of skin indentation and its derivatives feeding an integrate-and-fire spike generator, predicting spike timing to the millisecond for arbitrary stimuli.

TouchSim (Saal et al. 2017): extends this to the whole hand, with a skin mechanics model and thousands of simulated SA1, RA and PC afferents placed at realistic densities, so you can generate population spike trains for any contact.

Neuromorphic encoders: artificial fingertips whose sensor outputs drive Izhikevich-style model neurons to produce spike trains resembling afferents (Oddo et al. 2016) have been used to restore texture discrimination in amputees through nerve stimulation.
Transduction models: the Piezo2 channel and Merkel cell contribution are modelled as two-stage processes, a fast neuronal current plus a slower Merkel cell current that sustains firing.

blocks.text: What this means for your SNN

items: A tactile input layer should mix slowly adapting channels (static pressure, shape) and rapidly adapting ones (change, vibration). Using only one type of encoder loses half the signal.

Touch is a natural fit for the Thousand Brains idea that each column learns objects by moving a sensor over them: the fingertip is a small sensory patch whose location changes as the hand moves, and its afferents provide the 'feature at location' input.
For fast decisions, read out first-spike latency across the population rather than waiting for rates.
